lesson.menu_desc: Close calls at sea, told at the marina bar: what would have happened if, and what you should have done -- 13 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 10 -- Stories from the Water
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Eglis Roberto | Lesson 10 -- Stories from the Water

listenings.text: I have been sailing for forty years, and my worst day at sea was my own fault. We left the marina on a beautiful morning, and I did not check the forecast. In the afternoon, the wind changed, and a big gust hit us. We almost capsized. If I had checked the forecast, we would not have left that day. And if my friend Tom had not taken the helm, I think we would have hit the rocks. I should have reduced the sail much earlier, and I should have listened to the old fishermen at the bar. They told me the sky looked wrong. We got back in one piece, but I learned my lesson. Now I check the forecast twice.

People think the dangerous moment at sea is the storm. For me, it was a quiet night with no wind at all. Our engine stopped, and the boat started to drift towards the coast. I did not panic, but I was very close. Luckily, I had a radio, and the coast guard arrived in twenty minutes. If I had not had that radio, we would have run aground on the rocks. Honestly, I should have checked the engine before we left. It was making a strange noise all week. The young sailors at my club sometimes say I am too careful. Maybe. But I have never been reckless since that night.
